# Comments and doc comments

A comment is the part of the code the compiler does not run. That is why many people treat it as
free and write far too much. Nim has three forms with different rules, and one of them becomes
documentation. Placing it wrong makes the documentation disappear without a single error message.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can use the line comment `#`, the block comment `#[ ]#`, and the doc comment
`##` correctly, generate documentation with `nim doc`, and write examples that the compiler tests
through `runnableExamples`.
:::

## Line comments: `#`

The simplest form starts with `#`. Everything after it up to the end of the line is ignored.

```{.nim}
# This line is ignored by the compiler.
echo "comments do not run"  # this one too
```

```{.txt}
comments do not run
```

A line comment may stand alone at the start of a line, or trail after code. The compiler discards
both before it emits machine code, so there is no runtime cost. One thing to watch: a comment should
explain *why*, not *what*. `# add one` above `total += 1` tells you nothing.

## Block comments: `#[ ... ]#`

To disable several lines at once, use a block comment. It opens with `#[` and closes with `]#`.

```{.nim}
#[ This is a block comment.
   It can span several lines. #[ Nested blocks work too. ]#
]#
echo "after the block"
```

```{.txt}
after the block
```

Notice the `#[ Nested blocks work too. ]#` inside it. Nim counts depth: every `#[` adds a level and
every `]#` removes one. The inner block must close first, then the outer one. C does not work that
way; there `/* */` cannot nest. In Nim, disabling a block of code that already contains a block
comment still works.

## When a block is not closed

If `#[` is left open, the compiler never learns where the comment ends. Save the following as
`broken.nim`, then run `nim r broken.nim`.

```{.nim}
#[ this block never ends
echo "unreachable"
```

The compiler rejects it:

```{.txt}
main.nim(3, 1) Error: end of multiline comment expected
```

Read the message. `main.nim` is the file, `(3, 1)` is line 3, column 1, and `Error` means the build
stops. The text, "end of multiline comment expected", says the compiler reached the end of the file
before finding `]#`.

The position it reports is misleading at first. We wrote `#[` on line 1, but the compiler points at
line 3, the empty line after the last one. The compiler learns the comment was never closed only
when it reaches the end of the file. So the position it reports is where the compiler *noticed* the
problem, not always where the mistake was written. When you meet an error that points somewhere
unexpected, look a few lines earlier.

## Doc comments: `##`

The third form starts with `##`. This is not an ordinary comment, but documentation for the
declaration that follows. Save the following as `area.nim`.

```{.nim}
## Computes the area of a rectangle.
##
## The result is in the same unit as the arguments.
proc area(width, height: float): float =
  width * height

echo area(3.0, 4.0)
```

```{.txt}
12.0
```

As far as the program goes, `##` behaves like `#`: it changes nothing. What differs is that the
command `nim doc area.nim` collects every doc comment and writes an HTML file under the `htmldocs/`
directory, here `htmldocs/area.html`. Its contents are exactly the two lines of description above
the procedure.

The difference from `#` matters. A doc comment must use `##`; a `#` comment above a declaration does
not enter the documentation. So if you write `# Computes ...` above `proc area`, that note never
appears in the HTML even though it looks the same in the editor.

## `runnableExamples`: documentation that is tested

A doc comment is not only text. A `runnableExamples` block inside it holds code the `nim doc` command
actually compiles and runs. Save this as `double.nim`.

```{.nim}
proc double*(n: int): int =
  ## Doubles an integer.
  runnableExamples:
    doAssert double(2) == 4
  n * 2

echo double(21)
```

```{.txt}
42
```

Run `nim doc double.nim`. That command compiles the example block and runs it; if the `doAssert`
fails, `nim doc` stops with a non-zero exit code. This means documentation examples cannot go stale:
they fail as soon as the procedure's behavior changes. It is why many Nim library authors prefer
`runnableExamples` over static examples that are never tested.

One note: `nim doc` only runs `runnableExamples` on exported declarations (the ones ending in an
asterisk, like `double*`). A private procedure may still have a doc comment, but its examples are
not executed.

## Comments that are worth writing

With the three forms in hand, the question is when to comment. Three guidelines help:

- Explain the reason, not the mechanism. `# retry because the API returns 429 during deploys` is
  useful; `# loop three times` is not.
- Improve the names or structure if a comment starts papering over complicated code. Clear code needs
  no explanatory paragraph.
- Do not keep dead code in comments. Version history already keeps it; commented-out code only ages
  without being used.

## Exercises

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

1. Add a one-line comment to the first `echo` example that explains a reason, not a repetition of the
   code.
2. In the block comment of the second example, remove the nested block `#[ Nested blocks work too. ]#`.
   Does the program's output change? Why?
3. In the unclosed-comment example, on which line does the compiler report the error? Why not on the
   line where `#[` was written?
4. A procedure is annotated with `#` instead of `##` right above it. Does that note appear under
   `htmldocs/`? Explain.
5. Write an exported procedure with a doc comment and one `runnableExamples` block, then prove that
   `nim doc` fails when the block's contents are wrong.

## Summary

- `#` ignores the rest of the line; `#[ ... ]#` ignores a range and may nest.
- An unclosed block comment is reported at the end of the file, not where `#[` was.
- `##` is a doc comment; only this form reaches the `nim doc` output under `htmldocs/`.
- `runnableExamples` inside a doc comment is compiled and run by `nim doc`.
- A good comment explains a reason; dead code is not kept inside comments.
